102:| Cloud severance phase 1 (telemetry / update / notices) | this fork does not phone home. FOUR channels are cut at once and each is enforced at build time, not by configuration a merge can flip back. (1) **Telemetry keys are BANNED**: `assertNoTelemetryKeys` runs immediately after the repo-root `.env` load in `electron.vite.config.ts` and THROWS if `NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_KEY`, `SENTRY_DSN_DESKTOP`, `SENTRY_DSN_HOST_SERVICE` or `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` is set — a throw rather than a silent force-empty, because quietly rewriting a value the maintainer put in `.env` hides the disagreement instead of surfacing it. Banning `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` also disarms the two build-time sourcemap-UPLOAD plugins, themselves a phone-home to upstream's Sentry org. A `.env` carrying ports/URLs/workspace name keeps working. (2) **The bundled CLI's per-command ping is gutted**: `trackCommandInvoked` posted `api.analytics.captureEvent` to `SUPERSET_API_URL` on EVERY command via `commands/middleware.ts` — the one genuinely live per-command sink — and is now an empty body. Its signature, export and call site are unchanged on purpose: the middleware's `resolveAuth` chain is what the bundled `superset-cli` preset and the desktop startup shim depend on. (3) **Auto-update is hard-disabled**, layered: `FORK_AUTO_UPDATE_DISABLED` early-returns from `setupAutoUpdater`, `checkForUpdates` and `checkForUpdatesInteractive` INSIDE `auto-updater.ts` (call sites in `main/index.ts` churn on every merge, so the kill cannot live there); the feed constant is repointed from upstream's releases to the fork's; `electron-builder.ts` sets `publish: null` so no `app-update.yml` naming `superset-sh` is baked into the package even under `--publish never`; and ALL THREE "Check for Updates" entries — macOS app menu, tray, and the command palette's `actions.checkUpdates` — now permanent no-ops, are relabelled "Download Latest Release" and open the fork's releases page rather than being deleted or left as dead surfaces. They share ONE constant, `RELEASES_URL` in `shared/auto-update.ts`, which upstream pointed at `superset-sh/superset/releases` and which is repointed to the fork: it had no consumer at all before this, so a merge that started using it would have silently sent Windows ARM64 users to upstream's x64 build. Before this, only `IS_AUTO_UPDATE_PLATFORM` (mac/linux) stood between our Windows ARM64 users and upstream's x64 releases: one upstream line flip. (4) **CSP + CORS shim tightened surgically**: `posthog.com`, `sentry.io` and `sentry-ipc:` are gone from both `script-src` and `connect-src`, and the Windows CORS shim's `*.posthog.com` / `*.sentry.io` / `app.outlit.ai` patterns are deleted. `ws:`/`wss:`/`http://127.0.0.1:*` (terminals + host-service — removing these kills every terminal), `blob:`/`data:` (file previews) and the relay/api/electric entries are deliberately UNTOUCHED. `scripts/check-cloud-severance.mjs` proves all of it against the BUILT artifact set (whole set, never named chunks — see SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT), and that set deliberately includes the BUNDLED CLI: it ships as a compiled bun binary (`dist/resources/bin/superset.exe`), not a `.js` chunk, so the bundle scans cannot see it and its bytes are scanned separately for the analytics route name — otherwise the CLI channel would be the one phase-1 change enforced by source review alone. (`api.superset.sh` IS still in that binary and must be: the CLI's auth chain legitimately targets it in phase 1.) The gate also asserts the string `/api/desktop/version` appears in NO artifact: the poll-off is the one phase-1 behaviour whose markers live only in comments, so without that assertion a merge restoring the fetch would keep every marker and pass every other gate (api.superset.sh is phase-1-legitimate, so no hostname check can catch it). The gate is phase-scoped via an explicit `PHASE` constant because api/electric/streams/relay are still legitimately baked, and is frozen against build-repair edits alongside its allowlist. ENFORCEMENT does not rest on that freeze: the deciding invocation lives in `.github/workflows/build-arm64.yml`, which GitHub freezes for the whole run and which a mid-run repair therefore cannot reach, and the gate must leave a STAMP recording the sha it validated, the mode it ran in and how many assertions actually executed — the workflow re-checks all three against the sha it built, `mode=full`, and a floor of 11, so "the gate ran" is a fact the script has to produce rather than a string in an editable step. The floor is EXACT, not a lower bound with slack: a missing `apps/desktop/release` is a FAILURE rather than a skipped check, because a floor a skipped-packaging run can satisfy is not a floor. `--allow-unpackaged` exists for local post-compile runs and stamps `mode=partial`, which the workflow rejects, so the convenience cannot become a CI bypass. A failing gate writes no stamp at all. Phase 1 cut telemetry, updates and notices while sign-in, the api.superset.sh data plane and the relay stayed live; phase 2 cuts all three, and the app boots straight into a workspace with no login screen, no session to expire and no organization service to ask. **The identity is resolved from THIS DISK, once, and frozen** (`main/lib/local-identity/local-org.ts`): the organization id names the directory holding `host.db`, so it is ADOPTED from the one host database on the machine, recorded in `~/.superset/fork-local-org.json`, and never re-derived — a fresh uuid would not merely empty the sidebar, it would leave the companion's anti-rollback ANCHOR (`~/.superset/companion/state-anchor.json`, NOT org-scoped) ahead of a device index that lives INSIDE the org-scoped host.db, and `assertNoRollback` refuses that permanently, killing the one feature this phase exists to protect. Two host databases with no recorded decision FAIL LOUD rather than guess; `auth-token.enc` is consulted only as a tiebreak and is otherwise read-only, since every procedure that WROTE it is deleted. **The transport is severed at one choke point, not at 133 call sites**: `cloud-severed-link.ts` replaces the HTTP link on both cloud tRPC clients and opens no socket ever — it answers `v2Host.list`, `v2Host.listMembers` and `billing.activePlan` from local values (the host row must carry the same `getHostId()` the coordinator uses, or every host-keyed row belongs to a host nothing can reach; `listMembers` is not optional because the device picker intersects against it; the plan is unlocked because a paywall that never gets an answer locks features the user already owns) and REJECTS everything else with the procedure named — rejects, never throws synchronously, because `void ctx.api.x.mutate(...).catch(...)` sites would otherwise escape their own handler. The same Proxy shape severs the host-service's `ApiClient` and the bundled CLI's. **Deleted outright, not merely disabled**: the loopback `/auth/callback` route and the `superset://` auth deep link (both accepted a token from anything that could reach them, and post-severance that token names the identity the host-service runs under), the sign-in page's OAuth and dev-credential paths, sign-out (which used to stop every host-service — for a user who can no longer sign back in), the token-change listeners that tore the coordinator down, `useHostsPresence` (a raw `fetch` to the relay, invisible to both tRPC links — the exact fourth-channel class a choke point cannot see), and BOTH `connectRelay` mounts (`serve.ts` and the desktop child entry), which now REFUSE LOUDLY if `RELAY_URL` is set, because that value can arrive from the user's shell env and no absent-hostname assertion can prove a runtime dial impossible. ===== 1. ADOPTED ORG ID MECHANISM =====

ANSWER ON THE MYSTERY DIR FIRST: `~/.superset/host/00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000/` contains ONLY pty-daemon.log + pty-daemon-manifest.json — no host.db, no manifest.json, no workspaces. Do NOT adopt it; safe to delete manually. Adopting from auth-token.enc (below) excludes it by construction — one more reason adoption must NOT be a directory scan.

Resolution path (main process, boot):
1. New fork module `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/local-identity.ts`: async `resolveLocalIdentity(): Promise<{ token, organizationIds, activeOrganizationId }>`.
   - Call `loadToken()` (apps/desktop/src/lib/trpc/routers/auth/utils/auth-functions.ts:222-243). If token + non-empty organizationIds → ADOPT all ids verbatim. This machine: auth-token.enc exists in ~/.superset → yields 30e16b5a-e2af-4874-b126-acc7b3f17aa9.
   - Virgin install (no file, or token without cached org ids — the latter means membership was never cached so no host-service ever ran and no org-keyed data exists): mint `randomUUID()` (satisfies packages/host-service/src/env.ts:11 `z.string().uuid()` and coordinator SAFE_ORGANIZATION_ID_PATTERN host-service-coordinator.ts:133), token = `randomBytes(32).toString("hex")`, expiresAt = `"9999-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"` (must be Date.parse-able — auth-functions.ts:74).
   - Persist mint via ONE new function in auth-functions.ts doing a single `serializeAuthWrite` → `writeStoredAuth({token, expiresAt, organizationIds, organizationIdsRevision: 1})`, emitting NO events. TRAP: never compose saveToken + saveOrganizationIds — `saveToken` writes ONLY {token, expiresAt} (auth-functions.ts:258), silently WIPING stored organizationIds if run against an existing file, and emits "token-saved".
   - activeOrganizationId (multi-org): the id whose `~/.superset/host/<id>/host.db` exists, newest mtime wins; else `organizationIds[0]` (sorted — saveOrganizationIds normalizes, auth-functions.ts:304). Async fs only — startup sync fs is a live footgun (blank-window). Reconcile ALL ids regardless (coordinator already runs one service per org).
2. Boot wiring, replacing apps/desktop/src/main/index.ts:544-590: resolve identity FIRST; `setConfigProvider` returns `{authToken: identity.token, cloudApiUrl: "https://cloud-severed.invalid"}`; call `hostServiceCoordinator.reconcile(identity.organizationIds, ...)` directly. DELETE all three authEvents listeners (index.ts:575-590) — with signIn/signOut/persistToken/persistOrganizationIds/handleAuthCallback removed there are no emitters left, and deleting the listeners removes the token-saved→stopAll boot trap wholesale rather than working around it. authGeneration machinery goes too.
3. IPC to renderer: add `auth.getLocalIdentity` publicProcedure query on the existing auth router (apps/desktop/src/lib/trpc/routers/auth/index.ts:21) returning `{ userId: LOCAL_USER_ID, organizationIds, activeOrganizationId, token }`. Delete persistToken/persistOrganizationIds/signIn/signOut procedures (auth router :30,:42,:86,:123). LOCAL_USER_ID is a shared CONSTANT (e.g. "local-user") — it is never persisted; it only has to be consistent between the shimmed session and the severed link's synthetic v2Host.listMembers row (useAccessibleV2Workspaces.ts:319 null-guard, :711-717 accessibleHostIds).
4. Renderer: replace AuthProvider's hydration (AuthProvider.tsx:17-73 getStoredToken + better-auth refetch) with a query of getLocalIdentity feeding a module singleton; the authClient shim's `useSession()` reads it via useSyncExternalStore and returns a session shaped `{ user: {id: LOCAL_USER_ID, onboardedAt: <epoch>, deletionRequestedAt: null}, session: {activeOrganizationId, organizationIds, token} }` — satisfies every layout.tsx gate (:88, :269, :278, :282). Then the nine `env.SKIP_ENV_VALIDATION ? MOCK_ORG_ID : session…` ternaries collapse to plain session reads; do it as the plan's `useActiveOrganizationId()` helper for a mechanical diff. The nine sites: layout.tsx:90, CollectionsProvider.tsx:62, LocalHostServiceProvider.tsx:60+63, useKnownHosts.ts:42, useHostProjects.ts:53, useAccessibleV2Workspaces.ts:222, useWorkspaceHostOptions.ts:34, V1ImportModal.tsx:32, dev-chat.ts:79. LocalHostServiceProvider's whole persistMembership CAS loop (LocalHostServiceProvider.tsx:85-110) is deleted — main owns membership now; renderer never writes it.
Multi-org case: all ids reconciled → every org's host-service + host.db + companion pairing stays alive; renderer surfaces the ACTIVE one; the cloud org-switcher UI is cut, so switching = future nicety (config write + relaunch), not phase-2 scope. Single-org (this machine) is the real user.

===== 2. CHAT PANE =====

Load-bearing discovery: there are TWO chat stacks. The "chat" pane = CLOUD session registry (`cloudTrpc.chat.listSessions`) + LOCAL message runtime (mastracode via workspaceTrpc — useWorkspaceChatDisplay.ts:1-2 imports AppRouter from @superset/host-service). And "chat-v3" = FULLY local: sessions + messages in chat.db via `${hostUrl}/chat-v3/trpc` (packages/host-service/src/chat-v3/mount.ts — Claude/Codex adapters, zero cloud imports), but it is DEAD in the fork because its gate is a PostHog feature flag (usePaneRegistry.tsx:125 `useFeatureFlagEnabled(FEATURE_FLAGS.CHAT_V3) ?? false`) and P1 killed PostHog.

- Registry: `chat:` entry usePaneRegistry.tsx:531-557 + ChatPane imports :52-53; ChatPaneData stays in the types union (harmless) or goes.
- Openers: WorkspaceEmptyState.tsx:51 (id "chat" tile), useWorkspaceHotkeys.ts:67+289, useWorkspacePaneOpeners.ts:145, useDefaultContextMenuActions.tsx:87, usePRFlowDispatch.ts (addTab kind "chat"), useConsumeAutomationRunLink.ts:43+210+273+285 (dies with automations anyway). content.text:
Chat-v3 is a chat-shaped front-end over the **same agent CLIs you already run in terminals**:

- Harnesses are `claude-code` and `codex` (`chat-v3/mount.ts:38-44`) — it spawns your local Claude Code / Codex, same binaries, same logins.
- Sessions and messages persist in a local SQLite on your machine, not in Superset's cloud.
- Network traffic is only what those CLIs already make (Anthropic / OpenAI). Nothing to Superset.

So it's a terminal agent presented as a chat thread instead of a pty — no new accounts, no cloud.

One honest caveat: it's unreleased upstream, and packaged builds need its migrations folder shipped (`SUPERSET_CHAT_V3_MIGRATIONS`). If that's missing in the installer it'll fail to open — which I'd find on first launch, not now.

Fable's four MAJOR findings are fixed and re-verified — 55/55 tests, gate 20/20, 237 markers, 28 type errors (unchanged), REFERR clean.

What the fixes were, in plain terms:

1. **The CLI would have bricked for you specifically.** Your `config.json` holds a stored Google session from before this change. Once it expired, *every* command — including `ws`, `terminals`, `agents` — would have failed with "Session expired — run `superset auth login`", pointing at a login that no longer exists. A leftover session is now ignored rather than consulted.
2. **A fail-loud that failed silently.** If the org resolver ever had to refuse (two host databases, corrupt decision file), it threw inside the boot sequence where nothing catches it — no window, no dialog, app looks dead, and the one instruction that fixes it only in a log file. It now shows an error box and exits.
3. **Two overnight-reversion holes.** `cloud-trpc.ts` and the sign-in/layout files had no `FEATURES.md` markers, so a nightly merge could have quietly restored the cloud transport or the login screen while every gate stayed green. Markered now.
4. Smaller ones: `superset auth login` refuses honestly instead of hanging on a dead hostname, `whoami` answers locally, and the CSP check no longer misses a bare `wss:` sitting last in the directive.

Still waiting on the second Opus review before `/simplify` and commit.

Review target: `max`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Another Claude session sent a message:
<teammate-message teammate_id="rev-opus2" color="pink" summary="Full review: all 5 areas, EXPECTED=38 confirmed">
Reached all five areas. Dropping what you already fixed (boot dialog, auth-client sync throw, CSP gate regex, resolve-auth, FEATURES rows). EXPECTED answer at the bottom.

MAJOR — apps/desktop/src/main/lib/local-identity/local-org.ts:162 (persistDecision). Bare writeFileSync, non-atomic, while readPersistedDecision (line 138) treats any parse failure as permanent refuse-to-boot. Power loss / AV interception mid-write leaves truncated JSON; next launch throws and the app never opens until the user hand-repairs a file they don't know exists. The repo already has the right pattern two dirs away: packages/cli/src/lib/config.ts:49 writes tmp + rename. Fix: tmp file + renameSync.

MAJOR — local-org.ts:113 (and the CLI mirror, packages/cli/src/lib/local-org.ts:46). `entry.isDirectory()` on a readdir Dirent is false for a symlink or Windows junction pointing at a directory. A user who relocated ~/.superset/host/<orgId> to another drive with `mklink /J` — routine on Windows for multi-GB dirs — gets candidates.length === 0 → source "minted" → fresh uuid frozen to disk. Empty sidebar, and the companion anchor permanently ahead of a sequence-0 device index, so assertNoRollback refuses the bridge forever. Fix: accept `entry.isSymbolicLink() && statSync(full).isDirectory()` too, both resolvers.

MAJOR — local-org.ts:86 (UUID_PATTERN). The regex accepts only RFC-4122 v1–v5, strictly narrower than the validator the comment above it cites: packages/host-service/src/env.ts:11 is zod 4.4.3 `z.string().uuid()`, which accepts the wider RFC-9562 set (v6/v7/v8) and the nil uuid. A host dir the platform considers valid but this regex rejects is skipped at line 114 as if it did not exist → zero candidates → mint → the same permanent bricking. Conditional: I did not prove this platform ever issued a v7 id (yours on disk is v4). The defect is the resolver being stricter than the thing it quotes, where being wrong is unrecoverable. Fix: reuse the host-service predicate, or widen the version nibble.

MINOR — packages/host-service/src/serve.ts:128 and apps/desktop/src/main/host-service/index.ts:165. The RELAY_URL "refuse loudly" throw runs after installProcessSafetyNet() in the same listen callback, so safety.ts:54 catches it as uncaughtException and logs "staying up". A user with exposeHostServiceViaRelay on (coordinator sets childEnv.RELAY_URL at host-service-coordinator.ts:884) gets one error line per start and a service that keeps running. Effect is harmless — the dial is genuinely gone — but FEATURES.md claims a refusal and the callback's own comment says late installation is so "startup throws still reach main().catch"; this one does not. Fix: check env.RELAY_URL before serve(), or drop the throw and stop claiming a refusal.

MINOR — apps/desktop/src/renderer/lib/auth-client.ts:145. `property in LOCAL_MEMBERS` walks the prototype chain, so authClient.toString / .constructor / .valueOf / .hasOwnProperty resolve to Object.prototype members instead of the wall. Nothing touches them today; it is a hole in the "a Proxy cannot forget" guarantee. Fix: Object.hasOwn.

MINOR — apps/desktop/src/main/lib/egress-fence/egress-fence-core.ts:265. LOCAL_SCHEMES lists superset-app: but not the two fork protocols registered beside it at main/index.ts:320-336, superset-font: and superset-icon:. If custom-scheme requests ever reached the listener, superset-font://fonts/SF-Mono-Regular.otf parses to hostname "fonts", fails loopback, is not resourceType image, and gets cancelled — the bundled monospace fonts vanish. Measured against your phase-1 log (~/AppData/Roaming/Superset/logs/main.log, tracked=14): only http/ws://127.0.0.1:* and https://api.superset.sh were ever observed, no superset-app:/file:/blob:/data: despite the renderer loading over superset-app://. So custom-protocol traffic does not reach onBeforeRequest and nothing breaks today. The inconsistency is the finding — superset-app: is in the set for exactly this hypothetical.

MINOR — apps/desktop/src/renderer/index.html:34. connect-src allows ws://localhost:* and wss://127.0.0.1:* but not wss://localhost:* or http://[::1]:*. No live break (host-service is dialled at 127.0.0.1); asymmetric allowlist.

MINOR — dead imports from the session-read replacement: useKnownHosts.ts:3,5,7 (env, authClient, MOCK_ORG_ID all unused), useHostProjects.ts:5,8,12 (same three), useAccessibleV2Workspaces.ts:6,32, CollectionsProvider.tsx:11,16. CollectionsProvider.tsx:12 also inserts renderer/lib/local-identity above renderer/lib/auth-client, out of sorted order. No build impact, but `bun run lint` fails on unused imports and all four are merge hotspots.

MINOR — apps/desktop/src/renderer/lib/local-identity.ts:69. getLocalSession() builds a fresh object per call and authClient.useSession() calls it every render, so `session` has a new identity each render. PostHogUserIdentifier.tsx:42 keys its effect on [session, activeOrganizationId] and re-runs every render. Inert today (no PostHog key since phase 1, effect sets no state), but any future effect keyed on session that sets state loops. Fix: freeze both return values in module constants next to the existing cached org id.

EXPECTED = 38 is CORRECT, and your derivation is right. I counted reachable ok() sites in scripts/check-cloud-severance.mjs. Pre-release (what --allow-unpackaged measures) = 20: env vars 1, allowlist 1, seven assertAbsent at 543/553/562/568/577/585/602, CLI-binary needle scan 1 at 653, seven cloud-origin assertAbsent from the CLOUD_ORIGINS loop at 685, better-auth routes 1 at 696, FENCE-BLOCK positive 1 at 723, CSP 1 at 745. Release-dependent = 18: dist/release app-update.yml 1 at 810, assertAsarSetClean called exactly twice (844 packaged, 1059 installer-extracted) at 8 each — seven assertAbsent at 293/299/305/311/317/323/329 plus the CLI-in-asar ok at 376 — and the installer app-update.yml ok at 1079. 20 + 18 = 38. Every assertAbsent yields exactly one ok on a passing run (429-445), and assertAsarSetClean has no conditional skips: the no-CLI-found branch fails rather than skipping.

One correction to make while you are in that file: the workflow comment at .github/workflows/build-arm64.yml:203 decomposes 38 as "21 source/dist + 8 + 8 + 1". The sum is right, the split is not (it is 20 + 1 + 8 + 8 + 1). Whoever grows the gate next will derive the new constant from that comment, in a file frozen against self-repair, and block every nightly.

`packages/cli/src/lib/host/spawn.ts:115` → `getRelayUrl(api)` → `packages/cli/src/lib/host/relay-url.ts:10` queries the now-severed API client → rejects → `catch` at `:12` → returns `env.RELAY_URL` = `https://relay.cloud-severed.invalid` (`packages/cli/src/lib/env.ts:13`) → `spawn.ts:141` sets `RELAY_URL` in the child env → `packages/host-service/src/serve.ts:128` throws.

The refusal is not a guard against a stale shell variable. It is on the normal path, every time.

#### 5b. Both refusals are swallowed. They are `console.error` wearing a `throw`'s clothes.

Both throws sit *inside* the `serve()` listen callback (`packages/host-service/src/serve.ts:128`, `apps/desktop/src/main/host-service/index.ts:166`), and both callbacks open with `installProcessSafetyNet()` (`serve.ts:89`, `host-service/index.ts:115`). That installs:

```
process.on("uncaughtException", (error, origin) => {
    console.error("[host-service] uncaughtException — staying up", { origin, error });
});
```
— `packages/host-service/src/safety.ts:54-59`

The comment directly above the call says why the ordering exists: *"Install only after the server is listening so startup throws still reach `main().catch(...)` and exit with a non-zero code."* The refusal was placed on the wrong side of that line. It never reaches `main().catch` (`serve.ts:141`), never exits non-zero, and the manifest at `host-service/index.ts:151` has already been written — so the app believes the host-service is healthy, because it is.

Net effect: a log line, plus every statement after the throw in that callback is skipped. This violates fail-fast-and-loud while carrying a comment claiming to enforce it.

#### 5c. The desktop path can brick a user, with no in-app escape

`apps/desktop/src/main/lib/host-service-coordinator.ts:884` still does `childEnv.RELAY_URL = effectiveRelayUrl` when `exposeViaRelay` is true. `exposeViaRelay` is `row?.exposeHostServiceViaRelay` from local-db (`:809`) — a *persisted* value. Any user who ever flipped Settings → Security → expose-via-relay carries `1` in that column across the upgrade. And:

- `/settings/security` is now severed (`cloud-severed-routes.ts:50`) → redirect, no way to turn it off.
- `exposeHostServiceViaRelay` is in `EXCLUDED_SETTINGS_COLUMNS` (`packages/cli/src/lib/settings/registry.ts:338`) → `superset settings set` refuses it.

Because of 5b this currently degrades to a log line rather than a brick — but that is the safety net saving it, not the design. Fix 5b as written and this becomes "terminals do not start, and there is no supported way to fix it."

#### Deeper fix

The refusal belongs at the **producer**, not at two consumers:

- `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/relay-url/relay-url.ts:9` → `return undefined`. One line, one file, and `host-service-coordinator.ts:887` already does `delete childEnv.RELAY_URL` on the falsy branch. The desktop child can then never see it.
- `packages/cli/src/lib/host/relay-url.ts` → delete; drop `RELAY_URL` from the spawn env at `spawn.ts:141`.
- Keep exactly one child-side refusal, and move it to where it fails correctly: a `.refine()` on `RELAY_URL` in `packages/host-service/src/env.ts:22` and `apps/desktop/src/main/host-service/env.ts:14`. Env parse runs at import, long before `installProcessSafetyNet`, so it reaches `main().catch` and exits non-zero — genuinely loud, and it covers the user's-shell-env case the current comment is arguing for.

**Endorse:** `SeveredApiAuthProvider` (`packages/host-service/src/providers/auth/SeveredAuthProvider/index.ts:16`) constructed *in place of* `JwtApiAuthProvider` rather than leaving the real one inert. "An unused object that knows how to phone home is one call site away from doing it again" is the correct instinct and the correct depth.

**Endorse:** `packages/host-service/src/trpc/router/host/host.ts:26` making `getOrganization` synchronous and local. That call was the rare cloud read *not* already wrapped in a catch, so a severed client would have turned `host.info` into a hard error. Catching that is real depth.

---

### 6. The `FENCE-BLOCK` positive assertion — **WRONG mechanism. It is satisfied by a comment.**

`scripts/check-cloud-severance.mjs:711` tests `/FENCE-BLOCK/.test(artifact.text)` against `dist/main`. The premise — that absence cannot distinguish a blocking fence from a log-only one — is correct. The implementation does not establish presence of the behaviour.

**Verified against the built artifact.** The main bundle is not minified (no `minify` key anywhere in `apps/desktop/electron.vite.config.ts`; 797 surviving `//` comments in `apps/desktop/dist/main/index.js`). Three `FENCE-BLOCK` hits in that bundle:

```
33839:  `[egress-fence] (FENCE-BLOCK) BLOCKED ${details.resourceType} to ...`
33852:  // The literal "(FENCE-BLOCK)" is load-bearing, not decoration: the
33857:  `[egress-fence] (FENCE-BLOCK) installed on ${PARTITION$1} — BLOCKING ...`
```

Line 33852 is the source comment at `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/egress-fence/egress-fence.ts:141`, shipped verbatim. The assertion passes on that alone.

Worse, even the two string literals prove nothing about behaviour. Change `egress-fence.ts:112` from `cancel = shouldBlockEgress({...})` to `cancel = false`, leave both log lines untouched, and the gate is green while nothing is blocked. The assertion proves a string is in the file. Blocking depends on `shouldBlockEgress`'s return value reaching `callback({ cancel })`, which no artifact scan can see.

**Deeper fix — two layers, both already half-built here:**

1. **Behaviour is proven by the test, not the bundle.** `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/egress-fence/egress-fence-core.test.ts:334-401` is a genuinely good 7-case table over `shouldBlockEgress` (remote XHR blocked, loopback/`superset-app:`/`blob:`/`data:` allowed, favicon allowed, webview and unknown exempt, unparseable blocked). Run *that file* as a build gate step and the decision function's semantics are enforced, not its spelling. Per AGENTS.md the tree has no test gate — this is the case for a one-file exception, not for a string match.
2. **Wiring is proven structurally.** If a bundle assertion is kept, assert the *call*, not the marker: `/shouldBlockEgress\(/` present in `dist/main` and `callback\(\{\s*cancel` present. Still shallow, but it is at least a property of the code path rather than of a log line and a comment.
3. If the string assertion stays regardless, it must at minimum exclude comments — count only occurrences inside a backtick/quote literal — or the marker must be moved out of every comment in `egress-fence.ts` and `egress-fence-core.ts:258`. Note this fights the FEATURES.md marker gate, which pins `(FENCE-BLOCK)` to both files (`FEATURES.md:334-335`) and is satisfied by those very comments.

**Endorse:** adding `apps/desktop/src/main/lib/egress-fence` to `FROZEN_GATE_PATHS` (`scripts/ci-repair.sh:117`). Freezing the code an assertion stands guard over is exactly right, and it is what makes fix (1) sufficient — a repair agent can neither edit the decision function nor the gate.

content.text:
`/simplify` complete. All gates green after the fixes: 20/20 severance assertions, 237 markers, REFERR clean, 28 type errors (unchanged baseline), tests passing.

**Fixed — real defects the reviews caught in my work:**

1. **The relay refusal never refused.** Both `RELAY_URL` throws sat *inside* the listen callback, after `installProcessSafetyNet()` — whose `uncaughtException` handler logs "staying up". So it printed a line and carried on, after the manifest was already written. Worse: `superset start` resolved a relay URL through the severed API, fell back to the poisoned default, and would have hit that path *every time*. And a user who'd ever switched on "expose via relay" carries `1` in their local DB, on a settings page now severed — they couldn't have switched it off. Now killed at the producer (no relay URL is ever handed to a child) and refused in the **env schema**, which parses at import, before the safety net exists.
2. **The gate's one positive assertion was satisfied by a comment.** The bundle isn't minified, so `FENCE-BLOCK` matched the source comment explaining the marker — and even the log strings would have survived changing `cancel = shouldBlockEgress(...)` to `cancel = false`. It now asserts the wiring itself.
3. **~400 ms of blocked startup, twice.** `loadToken()` runs `scryptSync` synchronously before any window exists, and I was calling it eagerly to feed a tiebreak argument that's unreachable unless you have two host databases. Now lazy — and the host-service config path doesn't read the token at all, since nothing authenticates with it.
4. **Three ways the identity resolver could brick you:** a torn write of the decision file (now atomic), a Windows junction on the host directory reading as "not a directory" (now followed), and a uuid rule stricter than the validator it quoted (now aligned). Each failure mode ended in a minted id — which is the one outcome that permanently refuses the companion bridge.
5. The CLI's org lookup was quietly a *second* resolver that could disagree with the app; it's now purely a reader.

**Skipped, with reasons:** consolidating the five separate "this settings surface is severed" lists and moving the route guard to the root — both are worthwhile, but they're refactors of upstream-owned files late in a large change, and the current form is correct, just repetitive. Same for hoisting the duplicated severed-client helpers into `@superset/shared`. I'd rather land this verified and do those as a follow-up than churn 20 more files now.

Nothing is committed yet. Want me to commit to `cloud-severance-p2`?

content.content:
82:| Companion keep-awake | the phone/watch companion is worthless if the desktop sleeps mid-question: the answer path lives in host-service, which dies with the machine. The main process holds a power-save blocker (and suppresses app-initiated sleep) for exactly as long as the companion bridge is enabled AND running AND at least one device is paired, released the moment any of the three stops being true — it never pins the machine awake unconditionally, and it never blocks display sleep (screen off is fine; suspend is not) | `(KEEP-AWAKE)` |
84:| Companion pairing surface (desktop) | the entry point the phone's own instructions name — "open Superset and choose 'Pair a device'" — without which the companion feature cannot be bootstrapped at all: `openPairing` is reachable only from the desktop's authenticated tRPC surface, so nothing else can ever open the one 120 s LAN window. A row in Experimental settings reads `companion.status` and derives its own availability (off / enabled-but-failed-to-start / running are three different messages, because they need three different actions from the user) rather than offering a button that can only fail; it opens a fork-only dialog that renders the returned URI as a QR and counts the window down. The pairing code lives in the URL FRAGMENT, so the dialog is the only thing that ever holds it: it is never logged (diagnostics use only the non-secret `pairingRef`), never persisted, never an attribute, never selectable text (a screenshot of a QR expires in 120 s; a screenshot of the string does not), and the flow component is unmounted on close so the value dies with the dialog. Dismissing takes the 0.0.0.0:47611 listener down instead of leaving it up for the rest of the window, and every window operation is serialised because the bridge allows exactly one process-wide (an unserialised close could land after a later open and silently kill the new window). States are honest and bounded — opening / open-with-time-remaining / expired / failed-with-the-server's-reason, never an unbounded spinner. It does NOT claim "paired": the bridge exposes no completion signal to the desktop, so the expiry copy points at the phone, which does know. QR is drawn by a dependency-free byte-mode encoder (level M, versions 1-40, full mask selection) — a QR library would move `package.json`/`bun.lock` under the `(LOCK-REGEN)` gate — always dark-on-white regardless of theme, since an inverted symbol is unreadable to some decoders | `(COMPANION-PAIRING-UI)`, `(COMPANION-PAIRING-ENTRY)`, `(COMPANION-PAIRING-SEARCH)` |
86:| Companion pairing by 8-digit code (works off-LAN) | pairing used to have ONE way in — scan a QR and finish the exchange on 0.0.0.0:47611 — which a network that blocks phone -> PC traffic makes physically impossible, and a fresh install is then stuck forever because the ONE secret it is missing (the main Cloudflare service token) is delivered only by that exchange. `(REMOTE-CODE-PAIRING)` adds a second, additive way in: the desktop shows 8 CSPRNG digits grouped `1234-5678`, the user types them into the phone, and an SRP-6a (RFC 5054, 3072-bit group, SHA-256, `g=5`) exchange runs over the tunnel across three unsealed POSTs — `/v1/pair/begin` (metadata in, `pid` + a fresh 16-byte `pairSalt` out), `/v1/pair/kex` (`A` in, `B` out) and `/v1/pair/confirm` (`macPhone` in, the sealed step-4 envelope out). SRP, not the QR flow's X25519-plus-a-short-code: 8 typed digits are ~26.6 bits, so ANY scheme in which a passive observer can test a guess offline is broken by a laptop in minutes — mixing the code into HKDF alongside an X25519 secret does exactly that, because the observer holds both public keys and can score a guess without ever talking to the desktop again. A PAKE is the only construction that removes the offline test: the desktop stores `v = g^x mod N` where `x = H(pairSalt ‖ H("sc/v3 remote-pair":code))`, and NEITHER the code, `x`, `v`, nor any other offline-checkable derivative is ever transmitted, so every guess costs one online request against a window that is counting. Secret exponentiations (`g^x`, `g^b`, `(A·v^u)^b`) run on a FIXED 4-bit-window `BigInt` ladder — 64 windows of exactly 4 squarings + 1 multiply over a zero-extended 32-byte exponent, with a full-width `N+1` standing in for 1 so a zero nibble is not a cheap multiply — which makes the operation count independent of the exponent's bits; `node:crypto`'s `DiffieHellman` was implemented as a hardened OpenSSL exponentiation engine first and REMOVED after measurement, because constructing the group object costs ~2.4 s per exponent on the Electron/BoringSSL runtime this fork ships (an unauthenticated public request stalling the main thread), reusing one object retains the last secret exponent, and Electron's BoringSSL rejects the `KeyObject` import that would have avoided the constructor; the residual per-limb `BigInt` timing variation is stated rather than defended — `x` is computed locally at window open with no request in flight, and a fresh `b` is used for exactly two exponentiations before being dropped; `A` is refused unless it decodes to EXACTLY 384 canonical base64url bytes with `1 < A < N-1` and is never reduced mod `N`; that range check runs BEFORE the derivation is charged rather than inside the arithmetic, because a degenerate `A` is a free-to-forge constant (`PAD(0)`, `PAD(1)`, `PAD(N-1)`) and charging it first let a few dozen such packets exhaust the window's 64 new derivations without the desktop ever performing one — the order is validate, charge, derive; `u == 0` is refused; all of it fails as `pair_bad_key_agreement` rather than as a wrong code. Everything is domain-separated from the QR flow (salt `superset-companion/pair/v3-srp`, labels `sc/v3-srp device `/`confirm-phone`/`confirm-desktop`, an 825-byte `sc/v3-srp` transcript binding `pid ‖ deviceId ‖ PAD(A) ‖ PAD(B) ‖ pairSalt` — deliberately NOT RFC 2945's `M1`/`M2`, which would leave `pid` and `deviceId` unauthenticated — and `/v1/pair/confirm` bound into the step-4 AAD so a captured envelope cannot be replayed across flows), while the QR/LAN flow's wire bytes are unchanged BYTE FOR BYTE with pinned goldens proving it, and two cross-runtime differential vector cases (one with a leading-zero code) are frozen jointly with the Android client after both sides derived them independently — TypeScript/OpenSSL here, Java/BouncyCastle there — and agreed on every value. Grinding is ONLINE-only and bounded by, in order, the endpoint answering a bodyless 404 (byte-identical to an unknown path) unless a window is open, ONE window at a time process-wide across BOTH kinds, opened only by the person at the desktop, 120 s, single use, three bad MACs burning it, five confirms per window, a per-source request cap keyed on `cf-connecting-ip`, per-candidate ownership by that source, a MONOTONE per-window ceiling on TOTAL admitted requests (32x32, charged before the body is read, never refunded — the per-source table evicts its oldest bucket to keep the real phone reachable, which refunds that source, so the aggregate bound has to be stated separately to be true; the per-source rule is charged FIRST and the aggregate only once it passes, because charging the aggregate first let ONE address spend the whole window total on requests it was simultaneously being refused as a flood, locking out the phone the per-source rule exists to protect) and a MONOTONE ceiling of 64 genuinely-new key derivations per window (the candidate table evicts rather than refuses, so nothing else bounds how many exponentiations a flood can buy; a cached exact retry, a refused rewrite, a `begin` flood and every `confirm` cost nothing against it) — at most three guesses out of 10^8 per window a human deliberately opened. Reachability is HOST-scoped and fails closed: the three pairing paths are served ONLY on the dedicated public host `pair-superset.khaira.family` and by POST only (anything else there, trailing slash included, is a bare 404), those same paths are a bare 404 on the main host, an unknown or missing `Host` reaches nothing, and every ordinary route keeps its unchanged main Cloudflare Access JWT validation — the host/method/path gate is registered BEFORE the Access gate, which is what lets a phone with no Access token pair at all. There is no pairing-scoped Access token any more: one that ships inside a published APK is public by construction and was never a security boundary, so the PAKE is the boundary and the residual exposure — an unauthenticated public endpoint that a distributed flood can make expensive — is accepted and documented rather than papered over. Absent `~/.superset/companion/public-pair-host.json` the code flow is simply off (the QR flow is untouched) and `openRemotePairing` refuses with a message naming the file to create; a file that is present but malformed — or that names the MAIN application host — throws at start-up rather than silently falling back. A burned window is remembered for 60 s so the phone can be told "you burned it" instead of the bare 404 a never-opened window produces. Because that candidate table EVICTS oldest-first rather than refusing a newcomer, a phone can lose the candidate its own `begin` created — a flood arriving inside its `begin` -> `kex` gap displaces it while the window stays open and usable — so both remote steps answer `pair_unknown_candidate` there instead of the QR flow's `pair_wrong_peer`: the true advice is "repeat begin", and "something else answered instead of the desktop" reads as an attack for a case where nothing substituted itself. The missing candidate is itself the proof that `begin` must be repeated, so nothing is tombstoned to remember it. It is returned from `/v1/pair/kex` AND `/v1/pair/confirm` (eviction can land in either gap) and ONLY after the window, wire version, source and `pid` have all checked out — a wrong `pid`, a second source driving someone else's candidate, and a rewrite of an existing candidate all stay `pair_wrong_peer`, so the phone's Try again is never offered for a refusal a retry cannot fix. It stays remote-only (v1's codes are frozen and its shipped phone builds have no mapping for it), and it costs nothing — no confirm attempt, no MAC strike. Recovery is USER-INITIATED on the phone and deliberately never automatic: `begin` is unauthenticated, so a phone that silently re-begins on this code is an amplifier aimed at the public pairing host and buys nothing when the window is genuinely gone; confirm is never re-sent. The BODY is the contract rather than the status — the phone matches `{"code":"pair_unknown_candidate"}` and never reads the `400`, because a public edge can emit a 4xx of its own and this is the one failure whose message tells a user their code is still good, so an edge must not be able to talk them into resubmitting into a window that is not there; a body the phone cannot parse degrades to a generic "nothing was stored", which is why the shape is pinned to exactly one `code` field with `cache-control: no-store` on both paths. `(PAIR-CODE-ASCII)` asserts the minted code is exactly 8 ASCII digits before it reaches `srpComputeX`, whose password encoding is ASCII: a non-ASCII digit would silently become a verifier no phone could ever match while the user typed the right digits (the companion hit exactly this — `Char.isDigit` accepts Arabic-Indic and fullwidth digits its ASCII encoder then destroys). `(PAIR-TOKEN-BEFORE-PERSIST)` reads the Cloudflare Access token file BEFORE the window is consumed and the device persisted, because it is the only fallible read left in the completion path: reading it afterwards turned a missing or unreadable token file into the worst outcome the protocol has — the phone told `500 unknown` and honestly reporting that nothing was stored, while the desktop kept a device row nothing would ever use behind a window nothing could reopen. Failing first changes nothing at all, and the user finishes on the same still-live code once the file is fixed; everything after the persist is in-process deterministic crypto, so no post-persist failure remains that is not a programming bug. EVERY answer this host gives — success, refusal, and a body refused for size or syntax before parsing — is the pairing shape (`{code}` from a closed set) with `cache-control: no-store`; the shared bounded reader's sealed-protocol errors (`body_too_large`, `envelope_invalid`, `serverTimeMs`) are re-stated in that shape rather than escaping onto an unauthenticated host. The one-window slot is RESERVED before either opener awaits anything and filled only on success, so two opens racing cannot leave a live-but-unreachable window behind, a failed bind frees the slot, and a refused open never makes the bridge forget the live window it was refused for. Every derived key a candidate holds is OVERWRITTEN on every exit — close, expiry, eviction, burn and successful consumption alike — because dropping a map entry only makes key material unreachable, which is the one state nothing can ever clean up; the honest limits are stated in code, namely that JS `BigInt`s and strings (the displayed code, the Access secret) cannot be zeroed and that `BigInt` arithmetic is not constant time (the fixed-window ladder fixes the operation SEQUENCE, not the cost of each operation). The desktop dialog gains a mode toggle, renders the grouped digits (never selectable, never logged, never persisted, dropped with the dialog) and counts the same window down for either kind, with `pairingState` carrying the window's kind so the two modes cannot read each other's verdict | `(REMOTE-CODE-PAIRING)` |
96:| Only a person's keystrokes count as presence | the keystroke half of presence stamped on the FRAME TYPE — every `{type:"input"}` the renderer's terminal socket delivered — and xterm fires `onData` for two unrelated things: a person typing, and the terminal ANSWERING A QUERY the program on the other end sent (Device Attributes, cursor position, XTGETTCAP). xterm tracks the difference internally as `wasUserInput` and does not expose it on `onData`, so a TUI polling the cursor position registered as a user sitting at the desk several times a second with nobody in the room, and every companion push stayed held for as long as that program ran — indefinitely, and invisibly. The renderer now witnesses what only it can see: real keydown/paste/composition events, captured on the xterm CONTAINER rather than the textarea, because xterm dispatches `onData` synchronously inside its own textarea handlers and a listener beside them would miss the first keystroke of every burst. A frame is tagged `human: true` only when such an event happened within the tagging window, and the host-service stamps presence only for frames carrying it. It CANCELS NOTHING by design: this phase exists to prove the allowlist is complete before a later phase starts blocking. It logs ORIGIN ONLY (`scheme://host:port`) plus method, resourceType, initiator class and a first-seen timestamp with a count — never a full URL, path, query or fragment, because the companion pairing secret travels in a URL FRAGMENT and other URLs carry bearer tokens; an unparseable URL is recorded as `<unparseable>` rather than echoed. The exemption is an ALLOWLIST, not a denylist: an origin is logged ONLY for a request positively attributed to a non-webview webContents, and everything unattributable is counted-and-dropped under a second bare total. Initiator is resolved via `webContents.fromId`, which must tolerate an absent or destroyed id without throwing since the callback runs on every request. Dedupe is in-memory and BOUNDED (512 keys); at the cap it drops and says so loudly rather than evicting silently, because an eviction would make the log lie. Honestly scoped in-file: it sees session webRequests only — main-process fetch, electron-updater, `@sentry/electron`'s main transport (renderer Sentry too, IPCMode.Classic), the host-service child, the bundled CLI, spawned agent CLIs and the pty-daemon ALL bypass it, so a clean fence log proves the RENDERER is quiet, not the app. The build-time gate covers what this listener cannot reach | `(EGRESS-FENCE)` |

A `default`-mode log still contains full request URLs, so the enable path says so and tells the maintainer to delete the file afterwards | `(NETLOG-OFF)` |

/**
 * (PUSH-PRESENCE) How recent a presence signal has to be for the user to count
 * as AT THE DESK, and therefore for a blocked question to be held rather than
 * pushed.
 *
 * THE UX CONTRACT THIS NUMBER ENCODES. A question buzzes the phone if and only
 * if the user cannot already see it. Away at the moment of capture -> the push
 * fires IMMEDIATELY, with no delay of any kind, because latency is the entire
 * value of the feature. Present -> it is held, indefinitely, and is either
 * cancelled when they answer at the desk or fired the moment presence lapses.
 *
 * This replaced a blanket 180 000 ms delay (`PUSH_DELAY_MS`, deleted). That
 * delay was wrong in both directions at once: three minutes of dead air when
 * nobody was there to answer, and a buzz at 3:00 for a question the user was
 * reading at 2:59.
 *
 * 60 s is the width of "still here" for BOTH signals — a keystroke inside the
 * last minute, or an OS idle time under a minute. Long enough that reading a
 * paragraph of agent output does not read as absence; short enough that walking
 * away is noticed before the question goes stale.
 */
export const PRESENCE_WINDOW_MS = 60_000;

/**
 * (PUSH-PRESENCE) How old the desktop's presence beacon may be before it stops
 * counting as evidence of anything.
 *
 * The beacon is a POST from the Electron main process on its keep-awake tick
 * (15 s). Three missed ticks is a desktop that is gone, suspended, or on a build
 * that does not send them — none of which are proof the user is present, so past
 * this the decision degrades to keystrokes alone. That under-reports presence,
 * i.e. it errs towards PUSHING, which is the correct direction: an unnecessary
 * buzz is an annoyance, a suppressed question is a blocked agent nobody knows
 * about.
 *
 * Deliberately a little under 3 x 15 s so an ordinary late tick does not
 * straddle the boundary on every cycle.
 */
export const BEACON_FRESH_MS = 45_000;

export const PUSH_TTL_MS = 900_000;
/**
 * How long a captured question stays worth buzzing about, measured from the
 * moment it was ASKED.

 * `PushSender.schedule` needs an expiry, and the two obvious candidates are both
 * wrong: `PUSH_TTL_MS` is the FCM message's lifetime measured from SEND, and the
 * store's 24 h retention is about `already_resolved` answerability, not about
 * noise. Past this horizon an armed entry is dropped UNSENT — a question the
 * desktop slept through for six hours is answered at the desk, not buzzed about.

 * discards the frame without ever reaching the retract branch. A retraction
 * stamped with `now` is therefore self-cancelling — it is expired on arrival by
 * construction — and the notification it was sent to clear survives on the

content.text:
Not a bug — it's a deliberate design decision in your companion app, and both apps agree on it.

**What your desktop actually sent** (`host-service.log`): the recent ones are `lifecycle alert … kind=g`. `g` = ready-for-review (`"g" | "e"` in `lifecycle-alerts.ts:49`; `e` is a failure).

**Where that lands:**
- Phone: `kind=g` → channel `lifecycle_ready`, created `IMPORTANCE_DEFAULT` with **`enableVibration(false)`**. Its own description says: *"Nothing is blocked, so this does not vibrate."*
- Watch: `READY` → `vibrates = false`, asserted in a test (`LifecycleAlertPresentationTest.kt:69`).

So ready-for-review was built to be silent on both. What *does* buzz: blocked agents needing an answer (`IMPORTANCE_HIGH`, vibration on, and the only kind answerable from the phone) and agent errors (`kind=e`).

Your log shows both kinds firing — several `pushing questionId=… the user is away` entries earlier, then these silent `kind=g` ones.

One caveat if you think a *blocked-agent* alert also came through silent: Android freezes a notification channel's settings at creation. `createNotificationChannel` on an existing id changes nothing, so if that channel was ever muted — by you, or by an older build of the app — no code change can restore it. The app has a diagnostics screen that reports the questions channel's actual importance ("silent · never buzzes" etc.), which settles it in one look.

content.text:
Double-checked all four phone channels, the watch, and the repeat-alert logic. Everything matches the log — nothing is broken.

**Phone**
| Alert | Channel | Buzzes? |
|---|---|---|
| Blocked agent (needs your answer) | `questions`, HIGH | **Yes** — `enableVibration(true)` |
| Agent error / failed | `lifecycle_error`, HIGH | **Yes** |
| Ready for review (`kind=g`) | `lifecycle_ready`, DEFAULT | **No** — `enableVibration(false)`, deliberate |
| Lost contact | `liveness`, DEFAULT | Not set either way in code |

**Watch** agrees exactly: questions vibrate, `ERROR` vibrates, `READY` doesn't — pinned by tests at `LifecycleAlertPresentationTest.kt:69-70`.

**Why some vibrate and some don't, beyond the kind:** ready alerts are posted under the *terminal's* key with `setOnlyAlertOnce(true)`, so the 2nd, 3rd, 16th finish of the same chat updates one row silently — that's the `(ONE-BUZZ-UNTIL-READ)` design. Errors get a key per event, so two failures are two buzzes. Questions also set `setOnlyAlertOnce`, so re-posting the *same* question won't buzz again — a new question id is a new row and does.

So "this one vibrated" fits: that was a blocked-agent question or an error. The silent ones are ready-for-review.

**One thing I'd flag:** `liveness` ("Lost contact") is the only channel that never states its intent — no `enableVibration(...)` call, so it inherits whatever the platform defaults to. Every other channel says what it wants out loud. Worth making explicit either way.

* hold in the fallback case too, and that is exactly the case where the two devices cannot

data class LifecycleAlertText(
    val channelId: String,
    val channelName: String,
    val channelDescription: String,
    val title: String,
    val text: String,
    val vibrates: Boolean,
)

object LifecycleAlertPresentation {

    const val CHANNEL_READY = "companion.ready"
    const val CHANNEL_ERROR = "companion.errors"

    /**
     * The channel split, and the fallback wording for a kind.
     *
     * Strict: for callers that produced the kind themselves and where an unknown one is a
     * bug in this app, not a version gap. The Data Layer boundary is the opposite case and
     * uses [forKindOrNull].
     *
     * @throws IllegalArgumentException for a kind this build does not know — guessing would
     *   put wrong words on the wrist.
     */
    fun forKind(kind: String): LifecycleAlertText =
        forKindOrNull(kind) ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown lifecycle kind '$kind'")

    /**
     * The same lookup for the message boundary, where an unknown kind is a fact about
     * versions rather than a bug: a phone that has been updated ahead of this watch can
     * send a kind this build has never heard of. The caller drops it with a log — the
     * alternative is an exception out of the Data Layer listener, which takes the whole
     * watch app down and loses the kinds it *does* understand along with it.
     */
    fun forKindOrNull(kind: String): LifecycleAlertText? = when (kind) {
        WatchLifecycleKind.READY -> LifecycleAlertText(
            channelId = CHANNEL_READY,
            channelName = "Ready for review",
            channelDescription = "An agent finished. Nothing is blocked, so this does not buzz.",
            title = fallback(LifecycleKind.READY).title,
            text = fallback(LifecycleKind.READY).body,
            // A finished agent is not urgent: it will still be finished in an hour. The
            // buzz is reserved for things that are waiting on the user.
            vibrates = false,
        )

        WatchLifecycleKind.ERROR -> LifecycleAlertText(
            channelId = CHANNEL_ERROR,
            channelName = "Agent errors",
            channelDescription = "An agent stopped on an error and will not continue by itself.",
            title = fallback(LifecycleKind.ERROR).title,
            text = fallback(LifecycleKind.ERROR).body,
            vibrates = true,
        )

        else -> null
    }

content.text:
Changes are in. While Gradle runs, here's exactly what changed:

**Phone**
- "Ready for review" channel → `IMPORTANCE_HIGH`, `enableVibration(true)`.
- Channel id bumped `lifecycle_ready` → `lifecycle_ready_v2`, and the old one is deleted on start. This is the part that actually matters: Android freezes a channel's importance and vibration at creation, so on your already-installed app the old muted channel would have won forever. A new id is the only way it can start buzzing.
- Each finish now re-alerts (`setOnlyAlertOnce(false)` for ready). Rows are still keyed per terminal, so a chat that finishes sixteen times updates one card — but each update buzzes, because a silent update is indistinguishable from nothing happening.

**Watch**
- `READY` → `vibrates = true`, which also promotes its channel to `IMPORTANCE_HIGH` (the notifier derives importance from that flag).
- Same id bump, `companion.ready` → `companion.ready.v2`, old one deleted.
- Updated the test that pinned `READY.vibrates == false`.

Untouched: blocked-agent questions and errors already vibrated.

**One trade-off to be aware of:** you'll now feel every agent finish, not just blocked ones. If a workspace has several agents finishing in a burst, that's several buzzes. If it turns out noisy, the honest fix is per-terminal throttling rather than going back to silence — say the word.

Two things worth flagging:
- Your companion repo has **21 uncommitted files** of in-flight pairing/provisioning work (`ProvisioningInbox.kt`, SRP changes, etc.). I didn't touch, stash or commit any of it — my edits are in three separate notification files.
- I can't install to your phone or watch from here; these need rebuilding and reinstalling on both devices before you'll feel any difference.
